dailyBrief.text: Good morning — Solon gets a sunny, dry day today with a high near 72° after a clear 48° start, and Thursday warms further to about 76°. Overnight, the World Series refused to end: Tampa Bay scored twice in the 12th to walk off Milwaukee 4-3 and stave off a sweep, though the Brewers still lead 3-1 with Game 5 tonight at 8:08 PM. In Israel, the actual vote count kept both blocs short of a majority, with Netanyahu and Eisenkot staking rival claims, and at home the FEC's filing system was hit by hackers a week before the midterms. Tonight in Cleveland, the Cavs host Washington at Rocket Arena at 7 PM, and early in-person voting runs 7:30 AM to 7:30 PM today — with mailed ballots now needing to be received, not just postmarked, by 7:30 PM on Nov. 3.

With the baby due in early November, this is officially any-day-now week — hospital bags by the door.

With 93% counted, Netanyahu's bloc leads 53-48 in Israel — but neither side is close to a majority
items.summary:
The count in Israel moved further on Wednesday without producing a winner. With about 93% of ballots tallied, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties was projected at 53 seats, ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot at 48, with Arab parties holding 19. A majority in the 120-seat Knesset takes 61, and neither camp is near it.

The result is stronger for Netanyahu than Tuesday night's exit polls suggested, and it leaves him in place as caretaker prime minister while coalition talks play out. Eisenkot has argued that Netanyahu lost public support and should step aside, while Netanyahu has called for a strong right-wing national government and pointed to possible renewed joint action with the United States against Iran.

That stalemate matters well beyond Israel. A fragile or caretaker government prolongs uncertainty over Gaza, Iran and regional diplomacy, and markets reacted quickly — the shekel fell about 2% and Tel Aviv stocks dropped around 3% as the stronger-than-expected Netanyahu showing sank in.

What to watch: double-envelope ballots are counted Thursday, official results are expected November 4, and only then does the president begin consultations on who gets the first chance to form a government. Failure by both sides would point to yet another election in 2027.

items.title: Death toll in Spain's high-speed train crash rises to at least 30, with 80 injured
items.summary:
At least 30 people were killed on Wednesday when a high-speed train slammed into the back of another high-speed train that had stopped in central Spain, regional authorities said. The death toll climbed through the day from an initial 10, and officials warned it could rise further, with about 80 people reported injured.

The crash happened Wednesday morning in Toledo province, between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, on the line from Madrid to Seville. Both trains were carrying hundreds of passengers in the same direction when one ran into the stopped train, derailing two carriages and scattering wreckage down an embankment. Rail operator Adif suspended service between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Health Minister Monica Garcia said rescue crews were focused on reaching survivors and recovering victims from the two most damaged carriages, and she urged blood donations as hospitals across the region took in the injured. It is Spain's second major train disaster this year, which will put the safety record of one of Europe's flagship high-speed networks under intense scrutiny.

What to watch: investigators have not yet identified a cause. Early reporting points to a signal fault that had halted the first train, but officials have not confirmed that account.

items.title: Australia still on track to get U.S. nuclear submarines in the early 2030s under AUKUS, defence minister says
items.summary:
Australia remains on track to acquire its first nuclear-powered submarines from the United States in the early 2030s, Defence Minister Richard Marles said on Wednesday. He described the AUKUS partnership with the U.S. and Britain as moving at the pace needed to deliver what the three countries call the optimal pathway.

Marles spoke after meeting U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of ASEAN meetings in the Philippines, calling the alliance as important as it has ever been. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in August that the pact remained, in his words, full steam ahead.

The Virginia-class boats are the centerpiece of Australia's biggest-ever defence project and a key piece of allied strategy in the Indo-Pacific. Any slippage would ripple through shipyard schedules in three countries and through the region's balance-of-power planning.

What to watch: delivery depends on U.S. submarine production rates keeping up with both American and Australian demand, a constraint officials on both sides have flagged before.

items.title: Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede Brazil's runoff and says he will seek to annul the vote
items.summary:
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro said he will not concede defeat in Brazil's presidential runoff and will seek to have the election annulled. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won the vote, securing a fourth non-consecutive term in office.

Bolsonaro's stated objection centers on a Supreme Court ruling by Justice Cristiano Zanin that extended voting by two hours on election day, a decision he called unacceptable. His challenge now moves the contest from the ballot box into Brazil's courts and electoral authorities.

A refusal to concede in Latin America's largest democracy raises the risk of protests and a drawn-out legal fight, even though Brazil's institutions ultimately managed a similar dispute after the 2022 election. Markets and neighboring governments are watching for any sign that the challenge gains traction beyond Bolsonaro's base.

What to watch: separate reports on Wednesday said Bolsonaro's whereabouts were unclear after he was ordered to surrender his passports. Those reports were not confirmed in the Reuters account of his annulment plan, so treat them as developing.

items.title: Thousands rally outside Portugal's parliament over the housing crisis and recent police operations
items.summary:
Thousands of people rallied outside Portugal's parliament in Lisbon on Tuesday as lawmakers debated the government's draft 2027 budget. Protesters were demanding action on a housing crisis that has made Portugal one of Europe's least affordable places to live, and protesting recent police operations against housing activists.

Home prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017 and rents on new leases have nearly doubled over the same period, while wages have not kept pace, hitting younger people hardest. The rally followed police operations over the weekend that dismantled activist tent camps in Lisbon and Porto, drawing allegations of excessive force.

Protesters want the minority centre-right government to drop a bill that would speed up evictions and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first reading with the far-right Chega party abstaining. Portugal's internal affairs watchdog has opened an inquiry into the police operations, and prosecutors have launched a separate investigation.

What to watch: the budget debate gives the protest a direct target, and similar housing demonstrations have been spreading across Spain and elsewhere in Europe this year.

items.title: Germany opens the door to handing back offshore wind sites as developers buckle under costs
items.summary:
Germany's economy minister, Katherina Reiche, said on Wednesday that companies may be allowed to return offshore wind farm sites they previously won at auction, provided they pay a penalty to transmission system operators. The concession is a response to mounting economic pressure across the sector.

Rising financing costs, crowded sea areas and weaker revenue expectations have made many awarded projects hard to build. Tenders scheduled for this year were postponed until 2027 after an August 2025 auction drew no bidders at all, and big 2023 winners such as BP and TotalEnergies have since faced supply-chain inflation and shrinking expected returns.

The heads of eight of Germany's 16 states have written to Reiche asking for a one-time, legally secure return option, with the sites then re-tendered promptly and the original owners excluded from bidding again.

Why it matters: Germany is Europe's industrial engine and a bellwether for offshore wind. If flagship projects stall there, it signals that the economics of the technology — not just permitting — are now the binding constraint.

items.title: Senate control could hang in limbo for weeks after Election Day, Axios reports
items.summary:
Senate leaders may not know who controls the chamber until well into November, Axios reports, thanks to a cluster of very tight races and state-by-state counting rules that stretch out close contests.

The stakes of the delay are practical. A Republican majority would ease the pressure on Majority Leader John Thune to move quickly on nominations, while a Democratic majority would hand Minority Leader Chuck Schumer more leverage in the lame-duck session that follows the election.

If the chamber lands exactly at 50-50, the two leaders would have to negotiate a power-sharing agreement before the Senate can fully organize — a process that has slowed Congress before.

What to watch: which races are still uncalled on the morning of November 4, and whether mail-ballot and recount rules in those states push answers into the following weeks.

items.title: Justice Department breaks the pre-election quiet with lawsuits in Alaska and California
items.summary:
The Justice Department has broken the usual quiet period before an election with a string of politically sensitive lawsuits and moves, Axios reports. The biggest is in Alaska, where a preemptive DOJ suit asks a court to delay certification of the U.S. Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses narrowly to Democrat Mary Peltola — arguing that a second candidate with a nearly identical name, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., could confuse voters.

Alaska's Supreme Court has already ruled that the second Sullivan belongs on the ballot. In California, DOJ sued on October 15 to block ballots from more than 20,000 people it suspects are noncitizens and demanded counties set those ballots aside — a request a federal appeals court has already rejected once.

President Trump has said he personally directed the Alaska suit and would do anything necessary to ensure honest elections. The Department of Homeland Security told the Associated Press that ICE is not planning operations targeting polling places, and senior Democrats on the intelligence committees say they have seen neither the capability nor the intent for foreign interference with voting infrastructure, though some required pre-election intelligence reports have not arrived.

Why it matters: certification is the step that turns ballots into an official result. Fights at that stage can leave seats empty and public confidence shaky long after Election Day.

items.title: A rough day in court for the administration: grand jury declines a case, appeals court blocks the California ballot move
items.summary:
A series of courtroom setbacks landed for the Trump Justice Department on Wednesday. A grand jury refused to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, the 9th Circuit shut down the administration's bid to sequester 20,000 California ballots, and Alaska Republicans pushed back against the federal lawsuit aimed at their state's Senate certification.

Elsewhere on the docket, a federal judge extended her block on the administration removing trees at the East Potomac golf course in Washington, and a separate judge set a Friday hearing on former FBI Director Jim Comey's motion to dismiss the third indictment brought against him.

Individually, each ruling is a single case. Together, they show the courts — including grand juries made up of ordinary citizens — acting as the main brake on the administration's most aggressive pre-election and personnel moves.

What to watch: the Friday Comey hearing, and whether the Justice Department appeals the California ballot ruling with six days left before the midterms.

items.title: U.S. tells Middle East partners to prepare for a short, intense campaign against Iran after the midterms, WSJ reports
items.summary:
The United States has told several Middle East countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections, according to sources cited by the Wall Street Journal. The messages went out through diplomatic and military channels.

Two officials said the U.S. military is also sending an additional Patriot missile-defense system from Texas to Israel to strengthen its air defenses ahead of any operation. Separately, the head of the U.N.'s nuclear watchdog told the Security Council that there is no indication Iran has tried to repair or rebuild the nuclear facilities damaged in U.S. and Israeli strikes over the past two years, while urging Tehran to readmit inspectors.

The timing is the story: a campaign planned for after November 3 would avoid making a new war the final argument of the midterm campaign, while the Israeli election result — with Netanyahu's bloc ahead but short of a majority — shapes who would be America's partner in it.

What to watch: any public movement of additional U.S. forces to the region, and whether the administration briefs congressional leaders before the election.

items.title: Democrats lead the generic ballot by a wide margin as House forecasters eye a big popular-vote win
items.summary:
House Democrats appear to be flirting with one of the biggest popular-vote wins in decades, according to CNN's Poll of Polls, which has them leading the generic congressional ballot by 9 points. The last time either party won the House popular vote by at least 10 points in a midterm was 1986.

The polling reflects President Trump's deep unpopularity six days before the vote, and it lines up with the pattern in individual Senate races, where new surveys show contests in places like South Carolina tied and Democrats ahead in states the party rarely contests this closely.

A generic-ballot lead does not translate seat-for-seat — district maps blunt national swings — but a margin this size would put far more Republican seats in play than the party planned to defend this cycle.

What to watch: whether late polling in the Senate toss-ups moves with the national number, or whether ticket-splitting keeps the two chambers on different paths.

items.title: Fed is expected to hold rates at 3.75%-4.00% today — the real question is December
items.summary:
The Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged on Wednesday at 3.75% to 4.00%, with futures markets putting the chance of a hold at roughly 90%. The decision lands at 2 p.m. Eastern, less than a week before midterm elections dominated by the cost of living.

Officials signaled patience after raising rates a quarter point in September, their first hike since 2023. Inflation is still running well above the 2% target — consumer prices rose 3.7% over the year in September — driven not just by energy and tariffs but increasingly by strong demand, including from the AI buildout, and healthy consumer spending.

That mix has split the committee. Former New York Fed President William Dudley notes that some officials weigh financial conditions heavily and others do not, and several regional presidents are seen as possible dissenters in favor of a hike today. Chairman Kevin Warsh's press conference will be parsed for how the Fed frames that divide.

What to watch: markets already expect another hike at the December 8-9 meeting. Any hint that December is a close call, in either direction, will move stocks and borrowing costs this afternoon.

items.title: Microsoft and Alphabet report after the bell today, with options traders braced for 5%-6% swings
items.summary:
Two of the market's biggest companies report on the same afternoon as the Fed decision. Microsoft and Alphabet both post quarterly results after Wednesday's close, and options pricing implies a move of about 5.1% for Microsoft and 6.0% for Alphabet — roughly $27 a share and $19 a share respectively.

Analysts expect Microsoft to earn $4.73 a share, up 14% from a year earlier, on revenue of about $90.6 billion, with Azure cloud growth the number that matters most. For Alphabet, the forecast is $3.03 a share on revenue up about 25% to $127.9 billion, with management's comments on Search and AI competition likely to drive the reaction as much as the numbers.

Both stocks carry Strong Buy consensus ratings, but Alphabet's average price target implies more upside — about 33% versus 15% for Microsoft — and at least one analyst cut his Alphabet target ahead of the print while staying cautious on Search.

Why it matters: these two reports are the market's cleanest test of whether AI spending is turning into AI revenue. A miss from either would land on the same day the Fed decides rates.

items.title: Vertiv stock jumps as data-center orders more than double and the company raises its full-year outlook
items.summary:
Vertiv, which makes the power and cooling equipment data centers run on, delivered the kind of quarter AI skeptics keep asking for. Third-quarter sales rose 61% to $4.31 billion, adjusted earnings hit $2.21 a share against a $1.82 consensus, and organic orders more than doubled from a year earlier. Shares jumped close to 20% on Wednesday.

Management raised the full-year outlook with it: revenue guidance moved to $14.45-$14.85 billion and adjusted earnings to $7.10-$7.20 a share, lifting the revenue midpoint by $650 million. The adjusted operating margin expanded to 25.2%.

Vertiv sits on the practical side of the AI boom — chips are useless without electricity distribution and cooling — so its order book is a tangible check on whether hyperscaler spending plans are becoming real purchase orders. By that measure, they are.

What to watch: converting a swollen order pipeline into delivered, paid-for equipment. Bookings make the headline; deliveries and cash collection decide whether this rally holds.

items.title: Earnings split sharply: Boeing plunges 10.7% on a wider loss, while UPS and PayPal beat and rise
items.summary:
Tuesday's earnings tape sorted companies into clear winners and losers. Boeing shares plunged 10.7% after the planemaker reported an adjusted loss of $0.34 a share, wider than the $0.21 loss analysts expected, on revenue of $24.2 billion. Its commercial airplanes unit stayed in the red even as the overall loss narrowed sharply from a year earlier, and it carries a record $745 billion backlog it is struggling to convert into delivered jets and cash.

UPS went the other way, rising 5.8% after adjusted earnings of $1.69 a share beat the $1.63 estimate. The company has been deliberately shedding lower-margin Amazon volume in favor of more profitable parcels, and it raised its full-year revenue guidance to about $92.6 billion.

PayPal gained 2% as adjusted earnings of $1.45 a share comfortably beat the $1.31 consensus, even though revenue of $8.58 billion came in light. The company raised its full-year earnings outlook to about $5.60 a share. Freeport-McMoRan also beat, rising 1.2%.

Why it matters: this is a market rewarding cash conversion and punishing promises. Boeing's problem is not demand — it is turning the biggest order book in its industry into airplanes.

items.title: AI stocks climb again as the semiconductor rally builds ahead of Big Tech earnings
items.summary:
The AI trade is staging a comeback after weeks of heavy selling. The Nasdaq rose 1.18% on Tuesday while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index jumped 3.6%, and the move extended into Wednesday's premarket, with Micron up about 4.2%, Western Digital up 5.1% and AMD up 1.8%.

Record earnings from South Korea's SK Hynix — profit up more than sevenfold, with a $75 billion shareholder-return plan — helped lift memory stocks across the sector. Vertiv's blowout quarter and outlook raise added a second, independent confirmation that data-center spending is accelerating.

The rally now runs straight into its biggest test: Microsoft and Alphabet earnings after today's close, followed by Amazon on Thursday, all landing alongside a Fed decision.

What to watch: cloud growth rates and capital-spending guidance tonight. Chip stocks have priced in a strong answer, which leaves little room for a merely good one.

items.title: Logitech sheds about $2 billion in market value as margin worries overshadow a profit beat
items.summary:
Logitech shares fell 10% on Wednesday, wiping about $1.8 billion off the company's market value, even though the computer peripherals maker beat profit expectations a day earlier. The stock had gained about 12% this year before the results.

The problem is the outlook, not the quarter. Logitech guided to a gross margin of 41% to 42% for the December quarter, roughly 200 basis points below a year earlier, and analysts pointed to component inflation, rising freight rates and heavier marketing and research spending. Its non-GAAP operating income of $231 million had beaten both consensus and its own guidance.

One analyst called the selloff profit-taking after a strong run; another called it excessive given that a disruption at one of Logitech's chip suppliers in June is now largely contained. The disagreement itself shows how narrow the market's patience is with consumer hardware margins right now.

Why it matters: Logitech is a clean read on the everyday PC market, which remains soft. Even a beat-and-raise on profit could not protect the stock once margins pointed the wrong way.

items.title: World Series Game 5 is tonight: Brewers can win their first title, Rays must win to stay alive
items.summary:
The World Series resumes tonight at 8 p.m. Eastern in St. Petersburg, with Milwaukee one win from the first championship in franchise history and Tampa Bay needing three straight wins to complete a comeback no team has ever pulled off from 3-0 down in the Series. Game 5 airs on FOX.

The Rays forced tonight's game the hard way. Milwaukee took a lead in the top of the 12th inning of Game 4 on a Cooper Pratt home run, only for Tampa Bay to score twice in the bottom of the inning — aided by a costly throwing error — and walk it off 4-3, ending the Brewers' eight-game postseason winning streak.

Milwaukee has named hard-throwing right-hander Jacob Misiorowski to start Game 5. Tampa Bay had not named a starter by Wednesday morning and may piece together a bullpen game, after Nick Martinez — the original Game 5 option — threw two scoreless innings in relief in Game 4.

What to watch: if the Rays win, the Series returns to Milwaukee for Game 6 on Friday and a possible Game 7 on Saturday. Tickets for tonight started around $530-$728 on resale markets this morning.

items.title: Trump says he is ending Biden-era methane restrictions on oil and gas drilling
items.summary:
President Trump said Tuesday that his administration is terminating a Biden-era rule aimed at cutting methane emissions from oil and gas drilling. He announced the move at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, saying it would save companies and consumers billions of dollars and unlock 210 million barrels of oil — about 10 days of U.S. petroleum consumption.

The administration is framing the rollback as a response to high fuel prices amid the war in Iran, and as relief for small operators the president said were crushed by the regulations. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin had previewed the changes last month, including ending the Super Emitter Program, which requires companies to investigate and repair major methane releases, and setting looser standards for small wells.

Methane is the main component of natural gas and a far more potent planet-warming gas than carbon dioxide in the short term; scientists estimate it accounts for about a third of greenhouse-gas warming, and oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source.

Why it matters: cutting methane has been one of the fastest available levers for slowing near-term warming. Removing the rule trades that benefit for lower compliance costs, and the change is likely to be challenged in court.

items.title: EQT to buy Range Resources in a $13 billion stock swap, creating a natural-gas giant
items.summary:
EQT Corp. has struck a deal to buy Range Resources in a stock swap worth nearly $13 billion, Dow Jones reported Wednesday. The combination would create one of the largest natural-gas producers in the United States.

Both companies are major players in Appalachian shale, so the deal is a bet on scale: more contiguous acreage, lower per-unit costs and a stronger hand with the pipelines and buyers that move gas out of the region. It also arrives as demand for U.S. gas is being pulled upward by LNG exports and by power demand from data centers.

The same Dow Jones roundup flagged the week's other energy pressures: oil prices rising after Houthi militants targeted Saudi energy infrastructure, and refining margins at all-time highs as tight fuel markets make refineries the earnings engine for the oil majors this quarter.

What to watch: shareholder and regulatory review of a deal this size in a single basin, and whether other Appalachian producers answer with deals of their own.

items.title: Record king tides flood both coasts, closing roads in California, Florida and the Outer Banks
items.summary:
Exceptionally high king tides flooded coastal communities on both U.S. coasts this week, closing roads in California, Florida and North Carolina's Outer Banks. The flooding arrived on schedule with the astronomical tide cycle, but at levels local officials described as record-setting in several places.

King tides are the highest tides of the year, driven by the alignment of the sun and moon. When they coincide with onshore winds or storms, water pushes into streets, yards and low-lying neighborhoods that normally stay dry, stranding cars and forcing detours even on otherwise clear days.

Coastal planners treat these events as a preview: the water levels reached during a king tide today are close to what ordinary high tide will look like in coming decades as sea levels rise, which is why cities from Miami to San Francisco log and photograph them so carefully.

What to watch: whether the same communities flood again at the next tide cycle, and how much of the damage lands on roads and infrastructure rather than homes.

items.title: Opioid deaths fall to their lowest level since the emergency was declared in 2017, HHS reports
items.source: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
items.summary:
Opioid overdose deaths have fallen to their lowest level since the opioid crisis was declared a public-health emergency in 2017, the Department of Health and Human Services reports. The decline extends a multi-year improvement after deaths peaked earlier this decade.

Officials credit wider availability of naloxone, the overdose-reversal drug, expanded treatment access and sustained enforcement against illicit fentanyl supply. The improvement has been broad, though it has not been even — some communities and age groups are seeing far larger declines than others.

The milestone matters because it suggests the combination of treatment, prevention and interdiction can move a number that for years only went up. Public-health experts caution that the trend is fragile: a shift in the illicit drug supply, such as a new potent synthetic, can reverse gains quickly.

What to watch: whether state-level data confirms the national picture, and whether funding for treatment and naloxone distribution holds at current levels.

items.title: Residential cruise ship suspends its world voyage in Cambodia over fuel costs, stranding about 200 residents
items.summary:
A residential cruise ship — a vessel whose passengers live aboard full-time as it sails the world — has suspended its voyage in Cambodia because of soaring fuel costs, leaving roughly 200 residents without the home they paid for.

Residents of these ships typically buy or lease cabins for years at a time, selling houses on land to live at sea. A suspended voyage is therefore not a ruined vacation; it is the loss of a home, with personal belongings, routines and medical arrangements all built around the ship.

Fuel is one of the largest operating costs for any vessel, and prices have been elevated through the energy shock that followed the strikes on Iran. The operator's decision shows how that shock is reaching even niche corners of the travel economy far from the front lines.

What to watch: whether the operator refunds or rehouses residents, and whether other long-voyage and residential ships announce similar pauses.

items.title: Brown leads Husted 47-44 in Ohio's Senate race in a new Suffolk poll — and Acton leads Ramaswamy for governor
items.summary:
Ohio's U.S. Senate race remains a coin flip in its final week. A Suffolk University / USA Today Ohio Network poll of likely voters released Wednesday has former Sen. Sherrod Brown leading appointed Sen. Jon Husted 47% to 44% — inside the poll's 4.4-point margin of error. The same survey has Democrat Amy Acton leading Republican Vivek Ramaswamy 48% to 44% in the governor's race.

Brown's edge rests on independents, who break for him 52% to 24%. Two minor candidates — Libertarian Bill Redpath and independent Greg Levy — take about 1.6% each, and in a race this close that combined 3% could decide it. Outside groups are already working that angle: a GOP-backed organization has spent more than $2.2 million boosting Levy, while a Democratic-linked group has texted voters promoting Redpath over Husted. Levy's campaign called the effort highly undemocratic.

The race is on pace to set Ohio ad-spending records and could decide Senate control. Suffolk's polling director put the dynamic plainly: independents will determine the outcome in Ohio, and every independent who votes third-party makes the remaining ones harder to win.

What to watch: final-week advertising in the Cincinnati and Cleveland markets, and whether either campaign can pull the minor candidates' voters back before Tuesday.

items.title: Still holding an Ohio mail ballot? Signal Cleveland walks through how to make sure it counts
items.summary:
If you are still holding an Ohio mail ballot, the safest move now is to deliver it in person. Under Ohio's current rules, mailed ballots must be received by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday November 3 — a postmark no longer saves a late ballot — so dropping it at your county board of elections removes the mail from the equation entirely.

Early in-person voting continues at county boards this week: Wednesday through Friday, October 28-30, from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.; Saturday October 31 from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.; and Sunday November 1 from 1 to 5 p.m. There is no early voting on Monday November 2. Election Day polls are open 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

Voters in person must show an unexpired photo ID: an Ohio driver's license or state ID, an interim BMV form, a U.S. passport or passport card, or a military, dependent, National Guard or VA ID. Student IDs, mobile IDs and out-of-state licenses are not accepted.

Why it matters locally: Ohio has both a Senate race and a governor's race inside the margin of error. Ballots that arrive late do not count at all, which makes the delivery method — not just the vote itself — part of the result.

items.title: Browns have no plans to trade Shedeur Sanders, with the backup quarterback stuck to the bench
items.summary:
Shedeur Sanders is not going anywhere. The Browns have no plans to trade their backup quarterback ahead of the deadline, according to Mary Kay Cabot of Cleveland.com, even though Sanders has been stuck on the bench all season behind a resurgent Deshaun Watson.

Sanders recently hired an agent for the first time in his career — he went through the 2025 draft process without one, a decision often cited in his fall from projected first-rounder to the sixth round — and the hiring fueled speculation that he wanted a move to a team where he could play.

Cleveland's logic is longer-term. Watson is in the final year of his contract, and Sanders showed flashes as a rookie last season, throwing for 1,400 yards with seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions across eight starts after injuries forced him into the lineup. Keeping him costs little and preserves a succession plan.

What to watch: the November 10 trade deadline. A quarterback injury elsewhere could test Cleveland's resolve with an offer, but for now the 5-2 Browns are keeping their insurance policy.

items.title: At 5-2, the Browns are low-key buyers to watch before the trade deadline, ESPN insider says
items.summary:
First place changes the phone calls. ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler named the 5-2 Browns a low-key team to watch before the November 10 trade deadline, writing that Cleveland likes to make deals and could be a quiet buyer rather than a seller.

The shopping list Fowler sketched starts with defensive-line help, where depth is available around the league, and includes a versatile blocker at tight end or H-back — the Patrick Ricard role that offensive coordinator Todd Monken used in Baltimore — to support a run game that has become central to Cleveland's identity.

The Browns head to Pittsburgh on Sunday for a divisional showdown with the also-5-2 Steelers, a game that will say a lot about whether this start is a contender's start. Deadline urgency tends to rise or fall on results like that one.

What to watch: Cleveland has an open roster spot on the defensive front after losing Kalia Davis for the season, so a move could come even before deadline week.

items.title: Cleveland City Council votes 7-6 against reimbursing the Browns $1.1 million for stadium repairs
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council voted 7-6 on Monday to reject reimbursing the Browns $1.1 million for repairs to Huntington Bank Field — money the city is obligated to repay under the stadium lease, and which Mayor Justin Bibb's administration supported paying.

The repairs were unglamorous and essential: a failed sanitary pump, a sewer ejector pump failure, failed pipe insulation and an overhead door, among other work needed to operate the city-owned stadium safely. Council members voting no were blunt that the vote was about the Browns' planned move to Brook Park, not the plumbing.

Councilman Michael Polensek said residents feel sold out by the $100 million settlement that cleared the team's move, adding that the city is frustrated about losing both the Browns and the stadium. Council President Blaine Griffin, who voted to pay, warned that refusing a lease obligation invites legal bills larger than the reimbursement itself.

Why it matters: it is the first time in recent memory council has rejected a stadium reimbursement — it approved $2.6 million in repairs just last year. The Browns still expect to be repaid, so the fight now likely moves to lawyers rather than ledgers.

items.title: Guardians face a $9.6 million decision on Jo Adell — keep, trade or non-tender the power bat
items.summary:
Steven Kwan's future will headline the Guardians' offseason, but Jo Adell may be the harder call. Adell is entering his final year of arbitration, and MLB Trade Rumors projects his salary at about $9.6 million for 2027 — a big number by Cleveland's payroll standards.

The case for paying it is the player Adell became after arriving from the Angels: the right-handed power bat the organization spent years failing to develop internally, capable of protecting Jose Ramirez in the middle of the lineup. That profile is exactly what Cleveland's lineup has lacked.

The alternatives are to trade him now and get value back, or to non-tender him — offer no contract at all and let him become a free agent, saving the money but losing the player for nothing. For a team that just played in the ALCS, walking away from its one proven right-handed power source would be a difficult sell.

What to watch: the non-tender deadline forces a decision early in the offseason, and Adell's market — teams are always short on right-handed power — will shape what a trade could return.

baby.tip: Car-seat week: practice installing the Aria V2 base now, while there is no rush — click it onto the Vista frame once at home, check the level indicator, and route the seat belt or LATCH exactly as the manual shows. baby.fact: Newborns arrive with remarkably good hearing: they have been listening for months in the womb, and studies show babies in their first days already prefer their mother's voice over a stranger's — and even recognize stories or songs heard often before birth.
